Desegregation. The process of ending racial segregation in public institutions, most notably schools, following the principle of equal protection under law. Driven by the civil rights movement of the mid-twentieth century, it challenged the legal doctrine of "separate but equal" and required the integration of facilities, transportation, and services that had been forcibly separated by race. Desegregation remained incomplete and contentious decades after its legal mandate, representing one of America's most protracted social transformations.

Before desegregation could happen, the legal foundation for segregation had to be overturned. Plessy v. Ferguson in 1896 had established "separate but equal" as legal justification for racial segregation, creating a foundation for Jim Crow laws across the South. Brown v. Board of Education in 1954 declared separate schools inherently unequal and unconstitutional, reversing Plessy and serving as the legal mandate for desegregation.

Desegregation faced massive resistance in the South. Federal troops were deployed to Little Rock Central High School in 1957, and national guard intervention occurred at the University of Mississippi in 1962. Busing became the controversial practice of transporting students across district lines to achieve racial balance in schools. Beyond schools, desegregation extended to lunch counters, swimming pools, hotels, and public transportation through sit-ins, freedom rides, and legal action.

The challenge was nationwide, not merely Southern. Many Northern cities practiced de facto segregation through residential patterns and school district boundaries, complicating the desegregation process nationwide. White resistance often took organized forms, from White Citizens' Councils opposing integration to massive resistance movements that closed public schools rather than desegregate them. Martin Luther King Jr. championed nonviolent desegregation through marches and civil disobedience, becoming the primary leader of this struggle.
